Makkan [except verses 20, 23, 91, 93, 114, 141, 151, 152 and 153, which are Madinan]. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "Except six verses." Its verses number 165. [It was revealed after Surat al-Hijr.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*ja'ala* (to make, to place) takes one object when it means *ahdatha* (to bring into being) and *ansha'a* (to originate), as in His saying ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾; and it takes two objects when it means *sayyara* (to make into), as in His saying ﴿and they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Gracious, into females﴾. The difference between *khalq* (creating) and *ja'l* (making): *khalq* carries the sense of *taqdir* (determining measure). [Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] said: "The difference between *ja'l* and *khalq* is that *khalq* carries the sense of *taqdir*..." etc. Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: *Ja'ala* and *khalaqa* have occurred in the same context: ﴿and He created from it its mate﴾ and ﴿and made from it its mate﴾, which is clearly synonymous. However, the mind inclines towards the distinction which al-Zamakhshari has put forward. It is supported by the fact that *ja'ala* was never linked with the heavens and the earth, whereas *khalaqa* regularly was. In this verse, the attribution of *khalq* to the heavens and the earth, and of *ja'l* to the darknesses and the light, confirms the distinction between them. And Allah knows best.]

In *ja'l* there is also the sense of *tadmin* (implication), as in creating one thing from another, or making one thing into another, or transferring something from one place to another. Examples include ﴿and made from it its mate﴾ and ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, because the darknesses are of dense bodies and the light is from fire; and ﴿We created you in pairs﴾, and ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

If you say: why is *al-nur* (the light) in the singular? I say: for the purpose of referring to the genus, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the angel will be upon its sides﴾; or because the darknesses are many, since every kind of dense body has a shadow, and its shadow is darkness, unlike light, which is of one genus, namely fire.

[Zamakhshari's words continue: "If you say: on what is the clause ﴿then those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals﴾ conjoined?" Ahmad said: This second view is open to question, since conjoining it to the relative clause (*sila*) makes it fall under its ruling. If it were said, "Praise belongs to Allah, who ... those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals," it would not be grammatical, because the sentence would lack a returning pronoun. It may be said that the apparent noun *bi-rabbihim* has been placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of magnification and exaltation. The original sentence was: "the One by whom those who disbelieve ascribe equals" or "the One to whom those who disbelieve ascribe equals," with the extension of its occurrence as a relative clause, observing this original form. This is an objection from the standpoint of grammatical analysis. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there will come to you a messenger confirming what is with you"﴾, according to the one who reads *ma* as a relative pronoun rather than a conditional. For the clause "there will come to you" and what follows falls under the ruling of the relative clause, which requires a returning pronoun to the relative, and that is lacking in form, since the apparent noun has been placed where the pronoun should be. The original is: "then there will come to you a messenger confirming it." Thus the conjunction becomes correct and its falling under the relative clause is established by this method. But in this verse of al-An'am there remains an objection in meaning according to the stated grammatical analysis, namely that the sense becomes: "Praise belongs to Allah who ... those who disbelieve ascribe equals," and such a juncture right after praise is inappropriate, as you see. So the better view, and Allah knows best, is to conjoin it to the beginning of the speech, not to the relative clause. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

As for the first view, it is that it is conjoined to *al-hamdu lillah* (praise belongs to Allah), in the sense that Allah is deserving of praise for what He created, since He created it only as a blessing; then those who disbelieve in Him ascribe equals to Him, thus being ungrateful for His blessing. As for the second view, it is conjoined to *khalaqa al-samawat* (He created the heavens), in the sense that He created what He created, which none other than Him can bring about, and then they ascribe to Him what has no power over any of it. If you say: what is the meaning of *thumma* (then)? I say: it expresses the improbability that they should ascribe equals to Him after the clarity of the signs of His power. Likewise, His saying ﴿then you doubt﴾ expresses the improbability that they should doubt concerning Him after it has been established that He gives them life, causes them to die, and resurrects them.

Then He decreed a term (ajal): the term of death. And a specified term is with Him (ajal musamma): the term of the Resurrection. It has been said: the first term is the period between one's creation and one's death, and the second is the period between death and resurrection, which is the barzakh (the intermediate state). It has also been said: the first is sleep, and the second is death.

If you say: "An indefinite noun (al-mubtada' al-nakirah) whose predicate is an adverbial phrase (zarf) must be postponed," [[Mahmud said: "If you say, an indefinite subject whose predicate is an adverbial phrase must be postponed, etc." Ahmad said: There is nothing in the intention of this meaning that requires fronting. Yet "and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour" (wa-'indahu 'ilmu al-sa'ah) occurs in a context of magnifying it, and it is nonetheless postponed after the predicate in what precedes it: "Blessed is He to whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned." So the apparent meaning, and God knows best, is that the fronting occurred only because the speech is transmitted from another speech, and the original, and God knows best, was: "Then He decreed a term, and a specified term with Him," since both are decreed. When the speech was turned from the coordinating conjunction (al-'atf al-ifradi) to distinguish between the two terms, the second was raised as a subject (bi-l-ibtida') and kept in its place of fronting, and God knows best.]] then why was it permissible to front it in His saying "and a specified term is with Him"? I say: because it has been particularized by a qualifier, so it approaches the definite, as in His saying "a believing slave is better than a polytheist" (wa-la-'abdun mu'minun khayrun min mushrik). If you say: the common usage is to say "I have a good garment" (indi thawbun jayyid) and "I have a clever slave" (li 'abdun kayyis), and the like, so what required the fronting? I say: what required it is that the meaning is: "And what a specified term is with Him!", magnifying the matter of the Hour, and since this meaning was intended, fronting became necessary.

In the heavens: this is related to the meaning of the Name of Allah, [[Mahmud said: "In the heavens is related to the meaning of the Name of Allah ... etc." Ahmad said: These two noble verses are twins. The praise in the verse of al-Zukhruf occurs with the same qualities of praise as here: the power to restore, the sole knowledge of the Hour, and the oneness in divinity, and in His being the one worshipped in the heavens and the earth.]] as if it were said: He is the one worshipped in them. From this is His saying, ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God in the earth﴾ (43:84). Or: He is the one known for divinity, or the one singled out for divinity in them, or He is the one who is called Allah in them, [[he returned to his own words. He said: Or He is the one known for divinity, or He is the one who is called Allah in them, etc." Ahmad said: In all these interpretations, the expression uses the thing that necessarily implies something, to refer to its well-known attributes, as occurs in the verse:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

That is, the well-known and famous one. He built it on the principle that whenever his poetry is mentioned, the listener understands at its mention its distinguishing qualities of excellence, eloquence, and soundness of composition, because of its fame for these. So he limited himself to saying "my poetry," relying on the listener's understanding.]] without anyone associated with Him in this name. It is also permissible that ﴿Allah is in the heavens﴾ be a predicate following a predicate, meaning: He is Allah, and He is in the heavens and the earth, in the sense that He knows what is in them, and nothing of it is hidden from Him, as if His essence were in them. If you ask: What is the place of His saying ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾? I say: If you intend the one singled out for divinity, it is a confirmation of it, because the one whose knowledge equally encompasses the secret and the public is Allah alone. The same applies if you make "in the heavens" a predicate following a predicate. Otherwise, it is a new independent sentence meaning: He knows your secret and your open. Or it is a third predicate: ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾, of good and evil, and He will hold you to account for it and punish you.

Regarding "min" in "min āyah" (from any sign), it is for generalization (istighrāq, comprehensiveness). And "min" in "min āyāti Rabbihim" (from the signs of their Lord) is for partitioning (tab'īd, partial reference). The meaning is: no proof ever comes to them from among the proofs whose consideration, reasoning (istidlāl) and reflection (i'tibār) are obligatory, except that they turn away from it—leaving off consideration, paying it no heed, and not lifting their heads to it—due to the scarcity of their fear and their failure to reflect upon outcomes. ﴿Then they have indeed denied﴾: this is a response to an omitted statement, as if it were said: if they turn away from the signs, then they have denied what is the greatest and most momentous sign, which is the Truth, ﴿when it came to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an, by which they were challenged despite their excessive eloquence, and they were unable to match it. ﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock﴾, which is the Qur'an—that is, its reports and its circumstances—in the sense of: they will soon know what it was they had been mocking. It will become evident to them that it was not a matter fit for mockery, and that will be at the sending of punishment upon them in this world or on the Day of Resurrection, or at the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 6, verse 6:

"Makkana lahu fi al-ard" (he established him in the land): he made a place for him in it. Similar to it is "arrada lahu" (he gave him ground to stand on). From it is His saying ﴿Indeed We established him in the land﴾ [28:4]... ﴿Did We not establish for them...﴾ [28:6]. As for "makkantuhu fi al-ard," it means I confirmed him in it. From it is His saying ﴿And We had established them in that wherein We have not established you﴾ [46:26]. Because the two meanings are close, He combined them in His saying ﴿We had established them in the land as We have not established you﴾ [6:6]. The meaning is: We did not give the people of Makkah the like of what We gave ʿĀd, Thamūd and others, of physical stature, abundance of wealth, and reliance on the means of this world. "Al-sama'" (the sky) is the canopy, because water descends from it to the clouds, or the clouds, or the rain. "Al-midrar" means abundantly flowing. If you ask: what is the benefit in mentioning the creation of another generation after them? I answer: it indicates that it is not too great for Him to destroy a generation and lay waste their lands, since He is able to create others in their place to settle His lands with them, as in His saying ﴿and he does not fear its consequence﴾ [91:15].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 7–9:

A Book written on parchment (qirtas), on paper, and they touched it with their hands. He did not limit them to seeing [it], lest they say: [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "He did not limit them to seeing it, lest they say..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The apparent purpose of the addition of their touching it with their hands is to confirm the reading at close range, i.e., that they read it while it was in their hands and not at a distance from them, [which would be the reason] for their belief. Otherwise, the sense is not perceived by touch, so as to make the purpose of its addition the perception of it by two means, as is understood from the words of al-Zamakhshari.]] "Our eyes have been dazzled, and we are left with no excuse." They would say, "This is nothing but manifest sorcery," out of obstinacy and defiance of the truth after its manifestation. "Then the matter would have been decided": the matter of their destruction would have been decided. "Then they would not be reprieved" after its descent even for the blink of an eye. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, they would not be given respite after its descent even for the blink of an eye..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It is not fitting to make the cause of their being immediately destroyed the clarity of the sign in the descent of the angel, for this statement may give the impression that the signs whose belief was obligatory upon them were not clearer than the descent of the angel, and that is not the case. The correct view, and God knows best, is that the cause of hastening their punishment, given the supposed descent of the angel and their not believing, is that they asked for something on which the obligation of belief does not depend, since what the obligation depends upon is the miracle as a miracle, not a particular miracle. So when they were answered in accordance with their demand and it did not benefit them, they were then at the utmost firmness in obstinacy, which is suitable for the absence of respite, and God knows best.]] Either because, when they see the angel having descended upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his true form, which is a sign more clear and certain than anything, and then they still do not believe, as He said: "Had We sent down to them angels, and the dead had spoken to them, [even then] they would not have believed" (6:111), destruction would have been inevitable for them, as the People of the Table were destroyed. Or because the choice, which is the basis of obligation, would be removed upon the descent of the angels, so their destruction would be obligatory. [[He returned to his words. He said: "Or because the choice on which the foundation of obligation is built is removed upon the descent of the angel, so their destruction becomes obligatory. Or because when they witness the angel in his form, their souls depart from the terror of what they witness." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This last reason is strengthened by His saying: "Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man." Ibn Abbas said: "So that they could bear to see him and not perish from witnessing his form."]] Or because when they witness an angel in his form, their souls depart from the terror of what they see. The meaning of "then" (thumma), after mentioning the two matters, [[He returned to his words. He said: "The meaning of 'then' after mentioning the two matters is the decreeing of the affair..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This subtle point is among the excellences of his insights.]] is the decreeing of the affair and the absence of respite. He made the absence of respite more severe than the decreeing of the affair, because the sudden arrival of hardship is more severe than hardship itself. "And had We made him an angel," i.e., had We made the Messenger an angel as they proposed, since they used to say: "Why has an angel not been sent down to Muhammad?" At other times they said: "This is nothing but a human being like you" (23:24), and "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels" (23:24). "We would have made him a man," i.e., We would have sent him in the form of a man, just as Gabriel used to descend upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the most ordinary circumstances in the form of Dihya. [[Agreed upon, from the narration of Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, from Usama ibn Zayd, who said: "I was informed that Gabriel came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while Umm Salama was with him, and he began to speak; then he got up, and the Prophet of God said to Umm Salama: 'Who is this?' She said: 'Dihya al-Kalbi...' The hadith." And in al-Hakim, from the narration of Masruq, from Aisha, who said: "I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) conversing secretly while in my lap a man whom I took to resemble Dihya al-Kalbi. He said to me: 'This is Gabriel, and he sends you his greetings.'" And in al-Tabarani, from the narration of Qatada, from Anas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "Gabriel comes to me in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi." Anas said: "Dihya was a large, handsome, fair man." In its chain is Ufayr ibn Sa'dan, who is weak. And in Abu Nu'aym's Dala'il, from the narration of Safwan ibn Amr, from Shurayh ibn Ubayd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I saw Gabriel in the form in which he was created, and before that I used to see him in various forms, and most often I saw him in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi." Its narrators are trustworthy, except that it is mursal. Ibn Sa'd related through Yahya ibn Ya'mar, from Ibn Umar: "Gabriel used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi."]] Because they could not remain with the sight of the angels in their true forms. "And We would have confused them," i.e., We would have obscured for them what they obscure for themselves at that time. For when they see the angel in human form, they will say: "This is a human being, not an angel." If he says to them, "The proof that I am an angel is that I have brought the miraculous Qur'an, which declares that I am an angel and not a human," they would deny him just as they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). When they do that, they will be forsaken, just as they are forsaken now, and He will have no obligation toward them. It may also be meant: "And We would have confused them" at that time with the same confusion they now impose upon themselves in their disbelief in God's clear signs. Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa-labasna 'alayhim" with a single lam. Al-Zuhri read: "wa-lalabasna 'alayhim ma yalbisun," with shaddah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 11:

[[Mahmud said: "If you say, what is the difference between His saying 'fa-unzuru' and His saying 'thumma unzuru'... etc." Ahmad said: Clearer than this interpretation is to make the command to travel in both places one command, so that it becomes a cause of looking. Wherever the fa (fa) enters, it is to show causation; and wherever thumma (then) enters, it is to draw attention to the fact that looking is the purpose of travelling, and that travelling is only a means to it, and no more. And how far apart are the purpose and the means, God knows best.]] I say: He made looking caused by travelling in His saying "fa-unzuru" (so look), as if it were said: Travel for the sake of looking, and do not travel the travel of the heedless. As for His saying "siru fi al-ardi thumma unzuru" (travel in the land, then look), its meaning is the permission to travel in the land for trade and other benefits, and the obligation to look at the traces of those who were destroyed. He drew attention to this with "thumma" (then), because of the distance between what is obligatory and what is permissible.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 12:

Their saying ﴿To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ is a question of rebuke, and ﴿Say: "To Allah"﴾ is a affirmation on their part, meaning: it is Allah, there is no dispute between me and you, and you cannot ascribe any of it to other than Him. ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾, meaning He made it obligatory upon His own essence to guide you to knowledge of Him, and He set up for you the proofs of His oneness through what you yourselves acknowledge, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth. Then He threatened them for their neglect of reflection and their associating with Him what cannot create anything, by His saying ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾, so that He may recompense you for your associating others with Him. As for His saying ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾, it is in the accusative as a mode of censure, or in the nominative: that is, "I mean those who have lost their souls," or "you are those who have lost their souls." If you say: how did He make their not believing a consequence of their loss, when the matter is the reverse? I say:

Its meaning: those who have lost their souls in the knowledge of Allah, due to their choosing disbelief. Therefore they do not believe.

**وَلَهُ** is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with **الله** (Allah), so that ﴿To Him belongs what dwells in the night and the day﴾. **ما سَكَنَ** comes from *al-suknā* (dwelling), and its verb is transitive through **في** (in), as in His words ﴿and you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾. **وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ** means He hears every thing heard and knows every thing known, so nothing is hidden from Him of what the two (the night and the day) contain.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 14–16:

The interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) precedes ﴿ghayra Allah﴾ rather than the verb ﴿atakhidhu﴾, because the denunciation concerns taking something other than God as a protector (waliyy), not the taking of a protector as such. Thus it deserves to be placed first. A similar construction is ﴿Say: Do you command me to worship other than God, you ignorant ones?﴾ and ﴿Has God given you permission?﴾

﴿Fatir al-samawat﴾ is read in the genitive (bi-l-jarr) as an attribute (sifa) of God, and in the nominative (bi-l-raf') as a eulogy (al-madh). Al-Zuhri read it as ﴿fatar﴾. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "I did not know what ﴿Fatir al-samawat wa-l-ard﴾ meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I originated it (fatartuha)'" [[Narrated by Abu ʿUbayd in Gharib al-hadith, and in Fada'il al-Qur'an with a good chain (isnad), in which there is none but Ibrahim ibn Muhajir; it will come in the explanation of Fatir.]], meaning: I initiated it (ibtada'tuha).

﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ and ﴿He provides but is not provided for﴾, like the saying of God: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾. The meaning is that all benefits come from Him, and it is not permissible for Him to benefit from anything.

It is read ﴿wa-la yutʿamu﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. Ibn al-Ma'mun related from Yaʿqub: ﴿wa-huwa yutʿimu wa-la yutʿamu﴾, with the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, the pronoun referring to other than God. Al-Ashhab read ﴿wa-huwa yut'imu wa-la yut'imu﴾ with both verbs in the active. It was explained as meaning: "He feeds, and is not asked to feed." Al-Azhari reported ''atamtu'' with the sense of ''istatamtu'' (I asked for food), and similarly ''afadtu'' (I asked for benefit).

It is also permissible that the meaning be: He feeds at one time and does not feed at another, according to what is in the interest (al-masalih), as you would say: "He gives and withholds, extends and restricts, enriches and impoverishes."

﴿The first to submit (awwala man aslama)﴾: because the Prophet is the foremost of his community in Islam, like the saying of God: ﴿And I am commanded to this, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾, and like the saying of Moses: ﴿Glory be to You, I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾, and ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾. The meaning is: I was commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from associating partners with God.

﴿Whoever is spared the punishment on that Day, God has surely shown him mercy﴾: this is the greatest mercy, which is salvation. [[Al-Mahmud said: "The intended meaning is the greatest mercy, which is deliverance from the Fire... etc." Ahmad (al-Qunawi) said: What necessitates restricting the mercy, either by making it the greatest, or by making it the mercy of reward, is that if it were left unrestricted, the consequence would not exceed the condition, since it is known necessarily that averting punishment is some kind of mercy. It is remarkable that al-Zamakhshari validates restricting it to the mercy of reward on the grounds that averting punishment necessarily entails reward, while others validate this restriction on the grounds that averting punishment does not necessarily entail the attainment of reward, since it is possible that punishment is averted from someone without his being rewarded; thus the consequent conveys a meaning not understood from the condition. This is how al-Qunawi validated it. By my life, the principle of the Mu'tazila (who hold that human beings are either certainly destined for Paradise or certainly for the Fire, and ground this in reason rather than revelation) necessitates what al-Zamakhshari adopted.]] Like your saying: "If you feed Zayd from his hunger, you have done him a kindness," meaning: you have completed the kindness to him; or, "then you have admitted him to Paradise," because whoever is not punished must inevitably receive reward.

It is read ﴿man yuṣraf ʿanhu﴾ in the active voice, and the meaning is: whoever God averts from him on that day, He has shown him mercy, in the sense of: whoever God repels from him, and protects him. The one averted from is known, and the object (al-masruf) is omitted because it is known or has been mentioned before, namely the punishment. It is also permissible that ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ be governed by ﴿yuṣraf﴾ as a direct object, meaning: whoever God averts from him that day, that is, it belongs to him, then He has shown him mercy. This reading is supported by the reading of Ubayy, may God be pleased with him: ﴿man yuṣrifi Allah ʿanhu﴾.

If Allah touches you with harm, such as sickness, poverty, or any other of His afflictions, then none can remove it except Him. And if He touches you with good, such as wealth or health, then He is over all things Powerful, so He is able to sustain it or to remove it.

Above His servants: a depiction of subjugation and of exaltation through dominance and power, like His saying ﴿And We are above them, subduing [them]﴾.

Al-shay' (the thing) is the most general of the general terms (a'amm al-'amm): [Mahmud said: "al-shay' is the most general of the general terms, since it applies to everything that may be... etc." Ahmad says: his explanation that al-shay' is "that which may be known and spoken of" differs from both the Ash'ari and the Mu'tazili schools. The Ash'aris explained it as "the existent and nothing else," while the Mu'tazilis said: "and the known which may possibly exist." Thus they agreed on excluding the impossible. In general, this question is counted among the disciplines of kalam (theology) in one respect, but this discussion is linguistic, and the judgment in it belongs to the people of language. The apparent sense of their usage supports this: "I was angry at nothing," and "if he saw something other than a thing, he took it for a man." That al-shay' is applied only to the existent is shown by the fact that if al-shay' were everything that may be known, whether as nonexistent, existent, possible or impossible, then it would not be true to say of any matter that it is "not a thing." For this reason it is correct to say of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "a thing unlike other things," as if you had said: "a known being unlike other known beings." But it is not correct to say: "a body unlike bodies."

Wa-aradd: ayy shahid akbaru shahadatan, fa-wada'a shay'an maqam shahid li-yubalagh fi al-ta'mim. Qul Allahu shahidun baynì wa-baynakum yahtamilu an yakuna tamam al-jawab 'inda qawlihi Qul Allahu, bi-ma'na Allahu akbaru shahadatan, thumma ubtada'a shahidun bayni wa-baynakum, ayy huwa shahidun bayni wa-baynakum; wa-an yakuna Allahu shahidun bayni wa-baynakum huwa al-jawab, li-dalalatihi 'ala anna Allaha 'azza wa-jalla idha kana huwa al-shahid baynahu wa-baynahum, fa-akbaru shay'in shahadatan shahid lahu.

Wa-man balagha ma'tufun 'ala damir al-mukhatabin min ahl Makkah. Ayy: li-undhirakum bihi wa-undhira kull man balaghahu al-Qur'an min al-'Arab wa-al-'Ajam. Wa-qila: min al-thaqalayn. Wa-qila: man balagha ilayhi ila yawm al-qiyamah. Wa-'an Sa'id ibn Jubayr: man balaghahu al-Qur'an fa-ka'annama ra'a Muhammadan ﷺ.

A-innakum la-tashhadun: taqrir lahum ma'a inkar wa-istib'ad.

Qul la ashhadu: shahadatakum.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 20–21:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians. They recognise the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by his description and attributes, which are firmly established in the two Books, with a pure recognition, ﴿just as they recognise their own sons﴾ by their features and characteristics. They are not hidden from them, nor are they confused with anyone else. This is a testimony offered to the people of Makkah through the recognition of the People of the Book of him and of the soundness of his prophethood. Then He says: ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ — from among the polytheists and from among the People of the Book who deny — ﴿they do not believe in him.﴾ They combined two contradictory matters: they lied against Allah without any proof, and they denied what had been established by clear evidence and sound demonstration, when they said: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him], nor would our fathers﴾, and they said: ﴿Allah has commanded us to it﴾, and they said: ﴿The angels are the daughters of Allah﴾, ﴿and these are our intercessors with Allah﴾. They attributed to Him the prohibition of the baheerah and the saaibah. They went on to deny the Qur'an and the miracles, calling them sorcery, and they did not believe in the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 6, verses 22–24:**

﴿And on the Day We gather them﴾: its governing verb (nasibuhu) is omitted. The estimated sense is: "And on the Day We gather them, such-and-such will occur," and it is left unstated so that the vagueness itself serves as a warning. ﴿Where are your associates?﴾ means: where are your gods that you made partners with Allah?

His words ﴿whom you used to claim﴾ mean: whom you claimed to be partners. Both objects of the verb are omitted. It is recited (in a qira'a, a recitation) as ﴿Yahshuruhum, then He will say﴾ with the yā' in both places. This question is put to them as a rebuke. It is possible that they see their associates, but at the time when those associates cannot benefit them and the intercession they hoped for will not come, it is as if they were absent from them. They are kept from them at the time of rebuke so that they lose them at the very hour in which they had placed their hope, and so they see the place of their disgrace and regret.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 27–28:

"And if you could see" — its answer is omitted; its estimated sense is: "And if you could see, you would see a dreadful matter." "They will be made to stand before the Fire" — show it to them until they witness it. Or: they will look down upon it while it is beneath them, or they will be made to enter it, and thus they will know the measure of its punishment, from your saying "I made him understand (waqqaftuhu) such-and-such" when you have grasped and known it. It is also read "waqafū" (with the verb in the active form), from "waqafa 'alayhi wuqūfan" (he stood over it / came to know it). "Would that we could be returned!" — this is their wish, completed. Then they begin: "and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers," making a promise of faith, as if they said: "We would not deny, and we would believe," in an affirmative manner. Sibawayh compared it to their saying:

"Leave me, and I will not return" — meaning "leave me, while I do not return," whether you leave me or do not leave me. It is permissible for it to be conjoined to "we be returned" (nuradda), or to be a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense: "Would that we were returned, not denying and being among the believers," so that it falls under the rule of the wish (tamannī).

If you say: "His saying 'and indeed they are liars' refutes this, for one who wishes cannot be a liar." I say: this is a wish that has included the sense of a promise, so it is possible for denial to be attached to it, as a man says: "Would that God would grant me wealth, so that I would be generous to you and repay you for your kindness." This is a wish in the sense of a promise-maker. So if he were granted wealth and did not show kindness to his companion nor repay him, he would be a liar; as if he said: "If God grants me wealth, I will repay you for the kindness." It is also read "wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna" with the verb in the subjunctive (naṣb), by implying "an" (that) as an answer to the wish. [Maḥmūd said: "It is read 'wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna' in the subjunctive, with 'an' implied, as the answer to the wish..." Aḥmad said: The form of wish and the form of statement often alternate. Do you not see the saying of God, the Exalted, "And of them is one who covenanted with God: 'If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous'" up to "and because they used to lie"? This covenant was in fact a wish in the form of a statement, and God knows best. Even clearer is His saying in another verse: "And they will cry out therein: 'Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteous deeds, other than what we used to do.'" This is the wish itself, but in the explicit form of a promise and statement, and God is the Granter of success.]

Its meaning: if we were returned, we would not deny and we would be among the believers. "Rather, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before" — of their vileness and disgrace in their records and through the testimony of their limbs against them. Therefore they wished what they wished out of impatience, not because they were resolved that if they were returned they would believe. It has been said: this concerns the hypocrites, and that there appears their hypocrisy which they used to hide. It has been said: it concerns the People of the Book, and that there appears to them what they used to conceal of the truth of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood. "And if they were returned to the world after standing before the Fire, they would surely return to what they were forbidden of disbelief and disobedience. And indeed they are liars" in what they promised of themselves, that they would not fulfil.

Its meaning: if we were returned, we would not deny and we would be among the believers. It has been said: this concerns the hypocrites, and that there appears their hypocrisy which they used to hide. It has been said: it concerns the People of the Book, and that there appears to them what they used to conceal of the truth of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 30–31:

﴿وَلَوْ تَرَىٰ إِذْ وُقِفُوا عَلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ — "Stood (wuqifu) before their Lord" is a metaphor (majaz) for being detained for rebuke and questioning, just as a guilty servant is made to stand before his master so that he may be reproached. It has also been said: "They were made to stand over the recompense of their Lord." And it has been said: "They came to know Him with the fullest knowledge."

﴿قَالَ أَلَيْسَ هَٰذَا بِالْحَقِّ﴾ — This is a reply to one who says: "What did their Lord say to them when they stood before Him?" So it is said: "He said: Is this not the truth?" This is a declaration from Allah, the Exalted, that they are condemned for their denial.

﴿قَالُوا بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا﴾ — Their words, since they used to hear talk of the Resurrection and the Recompense, were: "It is not the truth, and it is nothing but falsehood," ﴿بِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾, meaning: because of your disbelief in meeting Allah, that is, in the arrival of the Hereafter and what is connected with it. This matter has been fully examined in other places.

﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا جَاءَتْهُمُ السَّاعَةُ بَغْتَةً قَالُوا يَا حَسْرَتَنَا عَلَىٰ مَا فَرَّطْنَا فِيهَا﴾ — Until (ḥattā) is the end-point for "they denied," not for "they lost," because their loss has no end. That is: denial kept persisting with them until their regret at the time the Hour came. If you ask: "Do they not feel regret at their death?" I say: since death is an occurrence of the states of the Hereafter and its preliminaries, it is counted among the kind of the Hour and is named by its name. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come" [narrated by Abu Shuja' al-Daylami in al-Firdaws from Anas with the wording "When one of you dies, his resurrection has come"; and al-Tabari from the hadith of Ziyad ibn 'Ilaqa from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, who said: "They say 'the Resurrection, the Resurrection,' but the resurrection of a man is only his death"; and from the narration of Sufyan from Abu Qays, who said: "I witnessed a funeral in which 'Alqama was present. When he was buried he said: As for this one, his resurrection has come."]. Or the arrival of the Hour after death is, because of its swiftness, like what happens without an interval. ﴿بَغْتَةً﴾ means "suddenly," and it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state, in the sense of "surprising," or as a verbal noun, as if it were said: "The Hour surprised them with a surprise."

﴿فَرَّطْنَا فِيهَا﴾ — The pronoun refers to the worldly life; its pronoun is brought though it has had no prior mention, because it is known. Or it refers to the Hour, in the sense: we fell short regarding its matter and in belief in it, just as you say: "I neglected (farraṭtu) so-and-so." From this is the phrase ﴿فَرَّطْتُ فِي جَنبِ اللَّهِ﴾.

﴿يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ — like His saying ﴿فَبِمَا كَسَبَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ﴾, because carrying loads on the back is the customary usage, just as earning is customarily attributed to the hands.

﴿أَلَا سَاءَ مَا يَزِرُونَ﴾ — "Evil is what they bear," meaning: evil is what they bear as their burden, like His saying ﴿سَاءَ مَثَلًا الْقَوْمُ﴾.

He made the works of this world into play and amusement, and occupation with what does not matter and yields no benefit, whereas the works of the Hereafter yield great benefits. His saying ﴿for those who fear God﴾ is evidence that everything other than the works of the God-fearing is play and amusement. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "wa-la-dar al-ākhirah" (and the abode of the Hereafter). It is also read: "taʿqilūn" with the letter *tāʾ* and with the letter *yāʾ*.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 33:

qad in qad na'lamu in the sense of "perhaps" (rubba), which comes to intensify and increase the action [[Mahmud said: "qad in qad na'lamu in the sense of rubba, which comes to intensify and increase the action, as in his saying: 'But he who is generous with wealth may indeed ruin his wealth.'" Ahmad said: Similar to it is His saying, "and indeed you know that I am the Messenger of God to you," for their knowledge of his prophethood is greatly increased and confirmed by the manifestation of his signs, until it establishes the proof against them by their combining two contradictions: harming him, and the firmness of their knowledge of his prophethood. And God knows best. Also among this is his saying:

"Indeed I leave the horn-tip yellowed at its fingertips."

The purpose is to express the meaning with something that suggests its opposite, as a warning that what follows the verse is nothing but a return to the opposite. This is one of the subtleties and marvels of the Arabic language.]], like his saying:

"A man of trust, wine does not ruin his wealth... but he who is generous with his wealth may indeed ruin it"

"A man of trust, wine does not ruin his wealth, but he who is generous with his wealth may indeed ruin it.

You see him, when you come to him, radiant, as if you were giving him what you are asking of him.

And if there were in his hand nothing but his own self, he would give it generously, so let the one who asks him fear God.

Who is like Hisn in wars, and who is like him in repelling injustice or in confronting one who attempts it?"

By Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, praising Hisn ibn Abi Hudhayfa. "Al-thiqa" is from "wathaqa," like "al-'idda" from "wa'ada." If the first verb is kasr and the second is fath, its origin is "wathiqa," the waw was dropped and the ta' was substituted for it; its meaning is what one trusts in, or the verbal noun is the act of trusting, i.e., he is constant in what one trusts in of noble character, never departing from it, as if it were his brother, or constant with respect to being trusted. The attribution of destruction to wine is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because it is its cause, and likewise its attribution to "nā'il," i.e., giving. "Qad" here is for intensification; otherwise it would not be praise. (2- Kashshaf- 2) You see him radiant, joyful of face, when you come to him asking, so it is as if you were giving him the wealth you seek from him. He exaggerates his description of generosity to the point that he would give up his soul if he had nothing but it, and on that he builds the command to his asker to fear God, lest He take his soul and cause it to die.

So "sā'iluhu" the first is annexed to its second object, and the second is annexed to the first. His saying "fa-man" is a rhetorical interrogative of denial, meaning no one is like him in wars, and no one is like him, prepared to deny injustice and reject it, to attempt and to treat and to seek. The pronoun in "yuḥāwiluhu" refers to "ḍaym," or to Hisn, or to "man." The poem is also transmitted in another version, as a description of Ma'n ibn Za'ida, and it is:

"They say: Ma'n has no zakat on his wealth. And how would wealth be purified by one who gives it away?

When a year passes, you will find in his house nothing of wealth except its mention and its gifts.

You see him, when you come to him, radiant, as if you were giving him what you are receiving."

"He has become accustomed to extending his palm, so that even if he wished to withdraw, his fingers would not obey him.

So if there were not in his hand... [the verse]"

"Jamā'iluhu" is in the nominative, going by the meaning, because the meaning left nothing but its gifts and its bounty, which he takes from him. "Basṭ al-kaff" is a metaphor for abundant generosity. "Anāmiluhu" means the parts of his fingers.]]. The "hā'" in "innahu" is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). "Layaḥzunuka" is read with fath and with ḍamm of the yā'. "Alladhī yaqūlūna" is their saying: "a lying sorcerer." "Lā yukadhdhibūnaka" is read with tashdid and takhfif: from "kadhdhabahu" when he made him a liar in his claim, and "akdhabahu" when he found him a liar. The meaning is that your being denied is a matter that returns to God, because you are His messenger, confirmed by the miracles. So in reality they do not deny you; rather they deny God by rejecting His signs. Therefore let not your grief for yourself distract you, even though they deny you while you are truthful, and let what is more important occupy you: your great concern at their rejection of God's signs and their contempt for His Book. Similar is the saying of a master to his slave, when some people humiliate him: "They have not humiliated you, they have humiliated me." In this manner is His saying, "Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God." It is also said: they do not deny you in their hearts, but they reject with their tongues. It is also said: they do not deny you, since you are, in their eyes, the truthful one known for truthfulness, but they reject the signs of God. From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him:

The Messenger of God ﷺ was called "the Trustworthy" [[I did not find it from him, but in al-Tabaqat from the hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayya, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ reached twenty-five years of age and had no name in Makkah except 'al-Amin'," and he also related it from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib similarly.]], so they knew that he did not lie about anything, but they used to deny. Abu Jahl used to say: "We do not deny you, for you are truthful among us; rather we deny what you have brought us." It is reported that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq said to Abu Jahl: "O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar, since there is no one here but us?" He said to him: "By God, Muhammad is truthful, and he has never lied; but if the sons of Qusayy take the standard, the watering, the guardianship of the Ka'ba and the prophethood, what then will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" So it was revealed. His saying "but the wrongdoers" is the placing of an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, to indicate that they were wrongdoers in their denial.

And indeed the messengers were denied, a consolation (*tasliyah*, comforting) for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) [[He resumed his words. He said: "His saying, ﴿And indeed messengers before you were denied﴾, is a consolation ... etc." Ahmad said: There is no indication in it, because it is also consistent with the negation of denial, and its placement then in terms of virtue is clearer, i.e., these did not deny you, so it is your right to be patient with them and their affair should not grieve you; and if the prophets before you were denied by their peoples and they were patient with them, then you, since they did not deny you, are more worthy of patience. So it is consistent, as you see, with both interpretations, but it is from a different aspect than the one he used as evidence, which brings closer what he chose: for such consolation has been stated explicitly in such as His saying ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾, so He consoled him regarding their denial of him by the denial of other nations of their prophets, and this is nothing but a good interpretation, matching reality, supported by parallels, and God knows best.]] This is evidence that His saying ﴿Indeed they do not deny you﴾ is not a negation of their denial of him, but is from your saying to your servant: "They did not humiliate you, but they humiliated me." ﴿They were denied and harmed﴾ for their denial and their harming. ﴿And none can alter the words of God﴾, meaning His promises, from His saying ﴿And certainly Our word has preceded for Our servants the messengers: indeed they will be the victorious﴾, and ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾, meaning some of their reports and stories and what they endured in patience against the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 35–36:

His people's disbelief and their turning away from what he brought weighed heavily upon the Prophet (ﷺ), so the revelation came: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they do not believe. You cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills.﴾ And if their turning away weighs heavily upon you, then if you are able to seek a shaft (nafaq) in the earth, a passage through which you can go down into what is beneath the earth, so that you may bring them a sign they would believe in, or a ladder (sullam) into the sky, so that you may bring them a sign from it, then do so. It means: you are not able to do that. The purpose is to show how eager he was for his people's Islam and how fervently he desired it, and that if he were able to bring them a sign from beneath the earth or from above the heavens, he would bring it, hoping for their faith. It has also been said: they were demanding signs, and he was keen that they would be granted what they asked for, so his eagerness for their faith intensified. So it was said to him: if you are able to do that, then do it, indicating that his eagerness had reached the point that, had he been able to do it, he would have done it, so that he might bring them the signs they had demanded, perhaps they would believe. It is also permissible that seeking a shaft in the earth or a ladder in the sky means bringing the signs themselves, as if it were said: if you were able to penetrate beneath the earth or ascend to the sky, you would do so, perhaps that would be a sign for you in which they would believe.

The answer to "an" (in ﴿an tabtaghiya﴾) is omitted, as when you say: "If you wish that we go to so-and-so to visit him..." And had Allah willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, by bringing a compelling sign, but He does not do so, because it would go against wisdom; so ﴿do not be among the ignorant﴾, meaning among those who are ignorant of this and aspire to what is contrary to it. [[Mahmud said: "By bringing a compelling sign, but He does not do so, because it would go against wisdom; so do not be among the ignorant, meaning among those who are ignorant of this and aspire to what is contrary to it." Ahmad said: This verse also serves as a decisive refutation of the Qadariyya in their claim that Allah willed to gather all people upon guidance, but it did not happen. Do you not see that the sentence begins with "law" (if/had), and its implication is the impossibility of its answer because of the impossibility of what follows it? So the impossibility of their being gathered upon guidance is due only to the impossibility of the will. Hence you see al-Zamakhshari interpreting the will as coercing them upon guidance by a compelling sign, under which faith would not be a matter of choice, so that he may establish that this aspect of the will did not occur, while the will to gather them upon guidance by their own choice is established and not impossible, but its object did not occur. These are among his concealed meanings and hidden places, so beware of them, and Allah is the Granter of success.]] ﴿Only those who listen respond.﴾ That is: those whom you are eager to make believe you are like the dead who do not hear. Only one who hears responds, as in His words: ﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾ and ﴿the dead, Allah will raise them﴾, an analogy for His power to compel them to respond, in that He is the One who raises the dead from their graves on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿then to Him they will be returned﴾ for recompense. So He was capable of giving life to these dead in disbelief through faith, while you are not able to do that. It has also been said that the meaning is: and these dead, meaning the disbelievers, Allah will raise them; then to Him they will be returned, and then they will hear. As for before that, there is no way for them to hear. [[His words "ila istima'ihim" (to their hearing) perhaps should be "ila isma'ihim" (to making them hear). (ʿ)]] It is also read: "yurja'un" (they will be returned) with a fatha on the yāʾ.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 37:

"Why has no sign been sent down to him?" Nuzzila (nuzzila) means the same as unzila (unzila). It is also read as an yunazzila (an yunazzila), with both the doubled and the single letter (nun with tashdid and without). that compels them to faith.

Like the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel and the like, or a sign which, if they deny it, the punishment will come upon them. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that Allah is able to send down that sign, and that there is a restraining wisdom that turns Him away from sending it down.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 38:

﴿Communities like yourselves﴾, written down: their provisions, their lifespans, and their deeds, just as your provisions, lifespans, and deeds have been written down. ﴿We have neglected nothing﴾, meaning we have left nothing out, and have not overlooked ﴿anything in the Book﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), ﴿of any kind﴾, meaning of that: we have not failed to record it, nor to set down what must be recorded of the matters specific to it. ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, meaning all the communities, of beasts and birds alike, so that He may recompense them and render justice between one of them and another, as is related: He will take retribution for the hornless sheep from the horned one. If you say: how is ﴿communities﴾ said with the singular ﴿beast﴾ and ﴿bird﴾? I say: since His words, ﴿There is no beast on the earth nor bird that flies on its wings﴾, indicate the sense of comprehensiveness (istighraq) and dispense with saying "there are no beasts nor birds", the words ﴿but are communities like yourselves﴾ were construed according to the sense. If you say: why not say "there is no beast nor bird"? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 40–41:

"Ara'aytakum" (tell me). The second pronoun has no place in i'rab (grammatical case), for you say: "Ara'aytaka Zaydan ma sha'nuh" (tell me about Zayd, what is his state). If you assigned the kaf a grammatical place, it would be as if you said: "Ara'ayta nafsaka Zaydan ma sha'nuh?" (did you see yourself, Zayd, what is his state?), and that is an incoherent statement. The object of the interrogation is omitted, and its estimated form is: "in ataakum adhabu Allahi aw ataktumu al-sa'atu man tad'un" (if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom will you call upon?).

Then He rebuked them with His words: "aghayra Allahi tad'un" (is it other than God that you call upon?), meaning: do you single out your gods for supplication in the matter that is your habit when harm afflicts you, "am tad'una Allaha dunaha" (or do you call upon God apart from them)? "Bal iyyahu tad'un" (rather, it is Him alone that you call upon), meaning: you single Him out for supplication, not the gods. "Fa-yakshifu ma tad'una ilayhi" (then He removes that to which you call Him), meaning: that which you call upon Him to remove, "in sha'a" (if He wills), meaning: if He wishes to bestow favour upon you and it is not a corruption. "Wa-tansawna ma tushrikun" (and you forget what you associate), meaning: and you abandon your gods, "aw la tadhkurunaha fi dhalika al-waqt" (or you do not mention them at that time), because your minds at that time are overwhelmed with the remembrance of your Lord alone, since He is the One able to remove harm and no other.

It is also permissible for the interrogation to be connected to His words "aghayra Allahi tad'un" (is it other than God that you call upon), as if it were said: "Aghayra Allahi tad'un in ataakum adhabu Allah?" (is it other than God that you call upon if the punishment of God comes upon you?).

If you say: if you connect the condition to it, what will you do with His words "fa-yakshifu ma tad'una ilayhi" (then He removes that to which you call Him) alongside His words "aw ataktumu al-sa'atu" (or the Hour comes upon you), and the dreadful events of the Hour do not remove [anything] from the polytheists? I say: He has stipulated the condition of will in the removal, with His words "in sha'a" (if He wills), signifying that if He did so, there would be a face of wisdom in it, except that He does not do it for another wisdom which outweighs it.

Al-Baʾsāʾ and al-Ḍarrāʾ: distress (al-bu's) and harm (al-ḍurr). It is said that al-baʾsāʾ is drought and hunger, and al-ḍarrāʾ is sickness and loss of property and lives.

The meaning: We sent messengers to them, they denied them, so We seized them (with affliction) so that they might humble themselves (yatadarra'ūn), i.e., become lowly and submissive before their Lord and repent of their sins.

﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ Its meaning is negation of humbling: as if it were said, "they did not humble themselves when Our might came upon them." But it came with "lawlā" (why not) to convey that they had no excuse for abandoning humility except their obstinacy, the hardness of their hearts, and their self-admiration in their deeds, which Satan had made attractive to them.

﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ of distress and harm, i.e., they abandoned taking admonition from it, and it did not benefit them or restrain them.

﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ of health, abundance, and every kind of blessing, so as to alternate for them between the times of harm and the times of ease, as a compassionate father does with his child, being stern with him at one time and gentle with him at another, seeking his reform.

﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾ of good things and blessings, they did not add to their joy and exultation anything of thanks or turning to repentance and apology.

﴿We seized them suddenly, and behold, they were despairing﴾ — "mublisūn" means bewildered and regretful, in despair.

﴿So the last remnant of the people was cut off﴾ — "dābir" means the last of them; not one of them was left, their root having been completely uprooted.

[[The word "wājimūn" in the Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-wājim" is one whose grief has become so intense that he holds back from speech. (ʿ)]] ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ — a declaration that praise is obligatory upon the destruction of wrongdoers, and that it is among the greatest blessings and the most abundant portions.

[[Maḥmūd said: "Praise here is a declaration of the obligation to praise upon the destruction of ... etc." Aḥmad said: A parallel to it is His saying, Exalted is He: "And We rained upon them a rain, so evil was the rain of those who were warned.
