Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 46:

If Allah takes away your hearing and your sight, by making you deaf and blind, and sets a seal upon your hearts, by covering them so that understanding and reason depart from them, who is the god other than Allah who could bring them back to you? (Here "bihi" refers back to the taking and sealing.) Yataikum bihi, meaning: yatikum bidhaka (He brings it back to you), treating the pronoun as if it were a demonstrative (ism al-ishara), or it refers to what was taken and sealed. Yasdifun means they turn away from the signs after they have become manifest.

Since suddenness is when a matter befalls without one perceiving it and without its signs appearing, it is said: "suddenly (baghtatan) or openly (jahratan)." And it is reported from al-Hasan: "by night or by day." It was also read "baghtatan aw jahratan" [[The phrase "baghtatan aw jahratan" is thus in Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi. In some copies of this book it appears as "baghtatan aw jahratan," and it is annotated: that is, with the ghayn and the ha' vowelled with a fatha/harakat. End of note (ʿ)]]. "Will anyone be destroyed" (hal yuhlaku): that is, will anyone be destroyed with the destruction of punishment and wrath, except the wrongdoers (al-zalimun)? It was also read "hal yuhlaku" with the yā' opened (fatha on the yā').

Mubashshirin (bearers of good news) and mundhirin (warners): whoever believes in them and in what they brought and obeys them, and whoever denies them and disobeys them. He did not send them so that He would be occupied with them and so that they would demand signs from Him after the clarity of their matter through decisive proofs, "and [whoever] amends" what he is obligated to amend of what he has been charged with.

He made the punishment a touch (*massa*), as though it were a living being inflicting upon them whatever pains it wills. From this comes their saying: "I suffered from him the *al-amarrayn* and the *al-aqwarayn*" (two bitter trials).

Where they used the plural form for rational beings: and His saying, ﴿When it sees them from a far place, they hear its raging and its roaring﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 50:

Meaning: I do not claim what is far-fetched for the intellects [[Mahmud said: "Meaning: I do not claim what is far-fetched for the intellects... etc." Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is built upon his earlier principle regarding the superiority of the angels over the prophets. By my life, the apparent sense of this verse supports it, and therefore he seized the opportunity to argue from it. And to avoid one saying: the verse was revealed only as a refutation of the disbelievers' statement, "What is wrong with this Messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has not an angel been sent down to him to be a warner with him, or a treasure cast down to him...?" The verse rebuts their words, "What is wrong with this Messenger that he eats food?" by saying that he is a human, and that is the nature of humans. He did not claim to be an angel, so as to be surprised at his eating food. In that case, it does not imply the superiority of the angels over the prophets, because there is no dispute that prophets eat food and that angels do not; so the distinction in this respect is agreed upon, and this does not necessitate a consensus that the angels are superior to the prophets. Likewise, their statement "or a treasure be cast down to him" is refuted by saying that he does not possess the treasuries of Allah, the Exalted, so as to bring them a treasure from them according to their demand; nor did he say that to them, so that the proof be established against him by it. In this verse, the order differs from the order in His saying: "The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the favoured angels."

Al-Zamakhshari said: Because they are higher than the prophets, he has postponed the claim of angelhood here after the claim of divinity, since divinity is more exalted and higher, while angelhood is lower. There is no purpose for this except the preface I have mentioned, and I have made the matter of advancing and postponing follow the context, for eloquence may in one place require the opposite of what it requires in another. Al-Zamakhshari did not express himself well in his saying: "divinity does not have a rank higher than the rank of the angels," for he made divinity one of the ranks, like angelhood. Such a generalization is not permissible. A "rank" (manzilah) is an expression for the place to which Allah causes the servant to descend, in elevation or otherwise; so applying it to divinity is a distortion. And Allah is the granter of success to what is right.]] that I say to you that with me are the treasuries of Allah, which are His distribution among creation and His provision, and knowledge of the unseen, nor do I say to you that I am an angel [[His words "who are the most noble kind" — that is, according to the Mu'tazilah; as for the people of the Sunnah, humans are more noble, as established in the discussion of tawhid. (Ali)]] of the angels, who are the noblest kind created by Allah, the most excellent of them and the nearest in rank to Him. That is: I have not claimed divinity or angelhood, for there is no rank above the rank of the angels beyond divinity, so that you would find my claim far-fetched and deny it. Rather, I claim only what is possible for many humans, namely prophethood. "Are the blind and the seeing equal?" is an example for the one who is misguided and the one who is guided [[He returned to his speech, saying: "The blind and the seeing are an example for the misguided and the guided..." Ahmad said: His words "or claims the impossible" mean the impossible, and for that reason he set against it "the straight," meaning the possible. That follows from the claim of divinity, since to claim it is not permissible by reason. As for one who claims angelhood, he is not to be compared with one who claims divinity regarding rational impossibility. It is permissible in terms of power that a human be made an angel and an angel a human, just as it is permissible that a human be made a prophet. The evidence for this permissibility is His saying: "And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man." This is so even though reason permits it in the power of Allah, the Exalted, because substances are alike, and the attributes subsisting in some of them may be made to subsist in all of them; so the attributes by which an angel is an angel may be created by Allah in a human, and the reverse. Its not occurring does not negate its soundness and possibility. And Allah is the granter of success.]] or for one who follows what is revealed to him and one who does not follow it; or for one who claims the straight, which is prophethood, and the impossible, which is divinity or angelhood. "Will you not then reflect?" — so that you do not be misguided like the blind. Or: so that you may know that I did not claim what is unbecoming for a human. Or: so that you may know that following what is revealed to me is something I cannot do without. If you ask: what is the grammatical position of "I know the unseen"? I say: it is in the accusative, coordinated with his words "with me are the treasuries of Allah," since it is part of what is said, as if he said: "I do not say to you this statement, nor this statement."

Concerning ﴿warn thereby﴾: the pronoun refers back to His saying ﴿what is revealed to me﴾. As for ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered﴾, they are either people who have entered Islam and affirm resurrection, but are negligent in their deeds, so that ﴿he warns them with what is revealed to him, that they may be God-conscious﴾, meaning that they enter the company of the God-conscious among the Muslims. Or they are the People of the Book, because they affirm resurrection. Or they are some of the polytheists whose condition is known to be such that, when they hear of the resurrection, they fear it may be true and that they will perish. They are among those from whom it is hoped the warning will take effect, unlike the rebellious among them, so he was commanded to warn these.

[Quotation of Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari): "Those who fear are either people who have believed, except that they are negligent in their deeds… etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This circumstantial clause (hal) would be necessary only if it were said, "warn thereby those who will be gathered," because without the circumstantial clause the command to warn would embrace everyone, whereas the intention is to restrict it to some.

But since it has been said, ﴿warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾, this statement stands independently. Its content is to restrict the warning commanded to the people who fear resurrection, either because they affirm it, or because they take precautions for themselves, so that fear leads them to reflective inquiry that results in certainty, unlike the obstinate who are determined in denial. Not every one who fears resurrection lacks an intercessor, for the monotheists all fear and they are interceded for. If by "necessary" is meant a condition the one who has it cannot be separated from, as in His saying ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾ [qā'iman], then this is based on his principle of denying intercession (shafa'a), for in his view every one who fears has no intercessor, since only the people of grave sins who do not repent, or the disbelievers, fear. All of them, in his view, are equal in having no intercessor. Where he has affirmed intercession, he has made it specific to an increase in reward, so only those who on his claim deserve reward by righteous deeds attain it, and intercession is useful for additional favor in accordance with what pleases him. Thus, in his view, such a person does not fear resurrection, because he deserves Paradise. Therefore he made the circumstantial clause necessary, since people are of two kinds: the non-opponent, whom the verse does not cover; and the fearful, who fears only because he has deserved punishment, so no intercession reaches him. This is among his hidden treasures and concealed storehouses, so be alert to it, and God grants success by His mercy.]

As for ﴿they will have besides Him no protector or intercessor﴾, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿that they will be gathered﴾, meaning: they fear that they will be gathered unhelped and without anyone interceding for them. This condition is necessary, because everyone is gathered, so the thing feared is gathering in this particular state.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 52:

He mentioned those among the Muslims who were not God-fearing (muttaqun) and commanded the Prophet to warn them so that they might fear God. Then he followed this with mention of the God-fearing among them, and commanded him to draw them near and honour them, and not to obey anyone who wished for them something other than this. He praised them, saying that they persist in calling upon their Lord, that is, in worshipping Him, and are constant in it. The intended meaning of "the morning and the evening" is continuity. It was also said that the meaning is: they pray the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. He marked them with sincerity in their worship by His words ﴿desiring His Face﴾, and "face" is used to express the essence and reality of a thing.

It is narrated that some of the leaders of the polytheists said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If you were to drive these slaves away from us," meaning the poor Muslims, namely Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, Salman and their like, may God be pleased with them, "and those whose outer garments of wool were ragged (they had only woollen cloaks), we would sit with you and converse with you." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am not one to drive away the believers." They said: "Then keep them away from us when we come, and when we rise, seat them with you if you wish." He said: "Yes," hoping for their faith. [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab at its end, and al-Wahidi in al-Asbab, by way of Abu Mushajja' ibn Rib'i from Salman, who said: "The hearts-to-be-reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Uyayna ibn Badr, al-Aqra' ibn Habis and their companions, and said: 'O Messenger of God, if you were to sit at the front of the mosque and push away from us these people, and those whose outer garments of wool were ragged, meaning Abu Dhar, Salman and the poor Muslims, who had no other garments than woollen cloaks, we would sit with you, converse with you and take from you.' Then God the Exalted revealed ﴿And restrain yourself with those who call upon their Lord﴾ up to His words ﴿for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up seeking them out. The hadith..." It is also in Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and Abu Nu'aym in the biography of Khabbab; and in Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, al-Bayhaqi also, and al-Wahidi, by way of Abu al-Kunud from Khabbab concerning God's words ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, desiring His Face; you are not accountable for their reckoning in any way, nor are they accountable for yours in any way, so that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers﴾, he said: "al-Aqra' and Uyayna came and found the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar and Khabbab, seated among some of the weak believers." He related it at length.]] It is also narrated that Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If you did so, we would see what they become." He said: "Then write a document to that effect." He called for a sheet and for Ali, may God be pleased with him, to write it, and then [the revelation] came down. So he threw down the sheet, and Umar apologised for his statement. [[I say: this is in the hadith of Khabbab mentioned just above, without the counsel of Umar and his apology.]] Salman and Khabbab said: "It was about us that it was revealed. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would sit with us and draw close to us until his knee touched our knees. When he wished to rise he would rise from us, and then it was revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself with those who call upon their Lord﴾, so he left off rising from us until we rose from him." He said: "Praise be to God who did not take me until He commanded me to restrain myself with a people from my community. Your living is with me and your dying is with me." [[I say: as for the hadith of Khabbab, from its beginning to his words "that you rise," it is in his hadith mentioned just above. As for the hadith of Salman, I mentioned it first. As for his words "And he said: Praise be to God ... to the end," it is in the hadith of Salman alone.]]

﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning in any way﴾, like His words ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ (26:113). That is because they had attacked their religion and their sincerity, so He said ﴿you are not accountable for their reckoning in any way﴾ after His testimony to their sincerity and their desire for the Face of God in their deeds, meaning: even if the matter is as they claim before God, you are only bound to take the outward appearance and to adopt the mark (sīma) [[His word "bi-sīmah" is perhaps "bi-simah." (ʿ)]] of the God-fearing. And if they have an inward state that is not pleasing, their reckoning is incumbent upon them alone and does not pass over to you, just as your reckoning is upon you and does not pass over to them, like His words ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ (6:164). If you say: Did His words ﴿you are not accountable for their reckoning in any way﴾ suffice, that He added to it ﴿nor are they accountable for your reckoning in any way﴾?

I say: the two sentences have been made as one sentence, and by them a single meaning is intended, which is the meaning in His words ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾; and this meaning is not complete except by the two sentences together, as if it were said: neither you nor they shall be held to account for the other's reckoning.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: they will not be held to account for your reckoning, nor will you be held to account for theirs, so that their faith would concern you and the eagerness for it would move you to drive away the believers, ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾, the answer to the negation, ﴿and be among the wrongdoers﴾, the answer to the prohibition. It is permissible that it be conjoined to ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾ in the sense of causation, because being a wrongdoer is caused by driving them away.

It was read: "bil-ghadwah wal-ʿashiyy" (in the morning and the evening, with the singular form of ghadāh).

And thus We tested some of them by means of others: such a great trial, similar to this one. We tried them, that is, We afflicted them with one another. This is because the polytheists used to say to the Muslims: "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" That is, He has favoured them with success in attaining the truth and with what makes them happy with Him, rather than us, though we are the leaders and the chiefs while they are the slaves and the poor. They said this in denial that people like them could be upon the truth and be favoured with good from among themselves, and similar to this is ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [38:8], and ﴿If it were good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [46:11]. The meaning of "We tried them so that they would say that" is: We forsook them [[The statement "We forsook them so they were tested" is interpreted in this way according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, that He, exalted is He, does not create evil. According to the People of the Sunnah, He creates evil as He creates good. (Ibn al-Munayyir)]] so that they were tested, to the point that their being tested became the cause of this saying, for none says the like of this saying except one who is forsaken and tested. ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ [6:53], that is, Allah knows best who will have faith and gratitude, so He grants them success in faith, and who will insist upon their disbelief, so He forsakes them and withholds success from them.

Say (to them), "Peace be upon you." This may be a command to convey God's greeting of peace to them, or a command to begin them with the greeting, honouring them and comforting their hearts. Likewise His words, "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," are among what he is to say to them, to gladden them and give them good news of the vastness of God's mercy and His acceptance of their repentance.

It has been read as "innahu" and "fa-innahu" with a kasra, as a resumption (isti'naf), as if mercy had been asked about and it was said: "Whoever among you does evil in ignorance..." And with a fatha, as a substitution (ibdal) for "mercy," with "bi-jahalatin" in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: his doing it while ignorant.

In this there are two meanings. The first: he is one who performs the act of the ignorant, because whoever does what leads to harm in the end, while knowing it or supposing it, is among the people of folly and ignorance, not among the people of wisdom and judgment. From this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed she said, on an evening when I visited her, / 'You acted ignorantly deliberately, though you were not ignorant.'" [[«على» here means «مع» (with), i.e. she said on the evening of my visit "you acted ignorantly" (jahilta), meaning you did the deed of an ignorant person, or you feigned ignorance and claimed it, with your deliberate intent, though you were not ignorant at the time of the act, or you were not previously ignorant of anything. (Ibn?) (ʿ)]]

The second: he is ignorant of the harm and injury connected with it. It is incumbent upon the wise not to proceed with anything until he knows its state and its manner.

It has been said: it was revealed concerning ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, when he advised accepting the unbelievers' request for what they asked, not knowing that it was a corruption.

And thus do We detail the signs, and [We do so] that the way of the criminals may become clear. It is also read as "wa-litastabīna" with the ta' and with the ya', with the subject "al-sabīl" in the nominative (since it may be masculine or feminine); and with the ta' addressing the Messenger, with "al-sabīl" in the accusative. It is said: istabāna al-amr and tabayyana, and istabantuhu and tabayyantuhu (both mean: the matter became clear / I made it clear). The meaning: "And thus, with this clear detailing, do We detail the verses of the Qur'an and summarize them in describing the states of the criminals: the one who has a seal upon his heart, whose Islam is not to be hoped for; and the one in whom one sees a sign of acceptance, yet who fears when he hears the mention of the Resurrection; and the one who has entered Islam but does not observe its limits. And that you may come to know their way clearly, so that you deal with each of them in the manner in which he ought to be dealt with—We have detailed that detailing."

I have been turned away and restrained, by the proofs of reason that were set within me and by the proofs of revelation that I have been given, from worshipping what you worship besides God. This contains a charge of ignorance against them, and a description of them as rushing headlong into what they were in without insight.

﴿Say: I will not follow your desires﴾: that is, I will not proceed in your way, the path you have taken in your religion, following desire rather than following evidence. This explains the cause by which they fell into error, and it alerts everyone who wishes to reach the truth and avoid falsehood.

﴿Then I would indeed be astray﴾: that is, if I followed your desires, I would be astray, and I would not be among the guided in anything. The meaning is that you are likewise.

When he had denied that desire is followed, he drew attention to what must be followed, by saying: ﴿Say: I am upon clear proof from my Lord﴾. The meaning of ﴿I am upon clear proof from my Lord﴾ and ﴿you have denied it﴾ is: I, from knowledge of my Lord and that there is no deity besides Him, am upon a clear argument and a true witness; ﴿and you have denied it﴾, you, in that you have associated others with Him. It is said: "I am upon proof concerning this matter," and "I am certain of it," when it is established for you by evidence.

Then he followed this with what indicates the magnitude of their denial of God, the intensity of His anger against them for that, and that they deserve to be seized [[The phrase "yughāfaṣū" means: to be seized unawares. It is said: "ghāfaṣtu al-rajul" meaning I seized the man by surprise. (End of quote.) (ع)]] with the annihilating punishment. So he said: ﴿What you are hastening for is not with me﴾, meaning the punishment they sought hastily in their saying: ﴿So rain upon us stones from the sky﴾. ﴿The judgment belongs only to God﴾ regarding the delay of your punishment. ﴿He relates the truth﴾, that is, He decrees the true decision in everything He decrees, including the delay and the hastening in its divisions. ﴿And He is the best of deciders﴾, that is, the best of judges.

It has been read: ﴿yaquṣṣu al-ḥaqq﴾ [[The phrase "yaquṣṣu al-ḥaqq" is read as recorded. Its apparent meaning is that the reading "yaquṣṣu" comes from qaḍāʾ (judgment), and it is the well-known reading. Let it be examined. (ع)]], that is, He follows the truth and wisdom in what He judges and decrees, from "qaṣṣa athar" (to follow the trace).

﴿If with me﴾, that is, within my power and capacity, were what you hasten for of the punishment, ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾: I would have destroyed you swiftly, out of zeal for my Lord and indignation [[The word "imtiʿāḍ" means: the extension of anger. Its meaning is given in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ع)]] at your denial of Him, and I would have rid myself of you quickly. ﴿And God knows best the wrongdoers﴾, and what wisdom requires regarding the nature of their punishment.

It has also been said: ﴿upon clear proof from my Lord﴾, that is, upon an argument from my Lord, which is the Qur'an. ﴿And you have denied it﴾, that is, the clear proof. The pronoun is in the masculine form according to the interpretation of "the clear proof" or "the Qur'an."

If you ask: with what is "al-ḥaqq" in the accusative? I say: it is an attribute of a verbal noun of "yaqḍī", that is, He decrees the true decree. It is also permissible that it be an object, from their saying: "qaḍā al-dir'a" when he made the coat of mail, that is, He makes and arranges the truth. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿yaqḍī bi-l-ḥaqq﴾ [[in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, "yaqḍī bi-l-ḥaqq" (He judges with the truth)]].

If you ask: why was the yā' dropped in the script? I say: in following the script the pronunciation follows it, and its dropping in pronunciation is due to the meeting of two quiescent letters.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 59:

He made the unseen to have keys, by way of metaphor (isti'ara), because keys are the means by which one reaches what is in the storehouses [[Mahmud said: "'Keys' is a metaphor, because keys are the means by which one reaches what is in the storehouses... etc." Ahmad said: To apply the notion of "reaching" (tawassul) to God, exalted is He, is not sound, for it gives the impression of a renewed arrival after distance, since the saying "Zayd reached such-and-such" is understood to mean that he arrived after effort and distance, and God, exalted, is far above that. The absent is like the present in His knowledge, and knowledge of what exists is knowledge of what will exist; it does not vary or differ. It is not for us to use such an expression except on firm ground. And God is the Granter of success.]] that are secured with locks and bolts. Whoever knows its keys and how they are opened has reached it; so He means that He alone is the one who reaches the unseen things, and none other reaches them, like one who possesses the keys to the locks of storehouses and knows how to open them, and so is the one who reaches what is in the storehouses. "Mafatih" is the plural of "miftah," which is the key. It has also been read "mafatih" (with a different vowel pattern), and it was said that it is the plural of "maftah" (with a fatha on the mim), which means the storehouse.

"Wa la habbatin" ... "wa la ratbin wa la yabisin" is conjoined (ʿatf) to "waraqa" [[He resumed his discourse, saying: "'Nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry,' is conjoined to 'a leaf' and is included in its ruling... etc." Ahmad said: The purpose of this repetition is to renew freshness for what comes after a long interval, because when it was conjoined to "a leaf" after the affirmative had been negated for the thing intended by knowledge in His saying "except that He knows it," and these conjoined items were included in the affirmation of knowledge, which is the intended point, and the distance was long, and the last of them was linked to the earlier affirmation, it was fitting to renew the covenant with the intended point. Then the eloquence customary in the Qur'an required renewal by another expression, so that the hearer receives it fresh and new, not wearied by repetition. This secret is only sought out by the one who masters the science of rhetoric (bayan), and the eloquent men are silenced. And God is the Granter of success.]] and is included in its ruling, as if it were said: "And nothing falls of any of these things except that He knows it." His saying "except in a Clear Book" is like a repetition of His saying "except that He knows it," because the meaning of "except that He knows it" and the meaning of "except in a Clear Book" is one. The Clear Book is God's knowledge, or the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). It has also been read: "wa la habbatun... wa la ratbun... wa la yabisun" with the nominative case. In this there are two possibilities: that it be conjoined to the place (mahall) of "min waraqatin," or that it be nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), its predicate being "illa fi kitabin mubin," as when you say: "No man among them and no woman, except in the house."

It is He who takes your souls by night. The address is to the disbelievers, meaning: you lie prostrate [[His saying "munsadhdhimun" means lying flat on the back, or turned onto the face, as the Sihah (lexicon) states. (ع)]] all night like corpses. And He knows what you have committed (jarahtum) by day, that is, the sins you have earned in it. Then He raises you up in it, that is, then He raises you from the graves, concerning that for which you have spent your lives, namely the sleep by night and the earning of sins by day, and for its sake, like your saying: "For what did you call me?" and he says: "For such-and-such a matter." That the appointed term may be fulfilled (li-yuqda ajalun musamma), which is the term He has specified and fixed for the raising of the dead and their recompense for their deeds. Then to Him is your return, which is the return to the place of reckoning. Then He will inform you of what you used to do, in your night and in your day.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 61–62:

﴿Hafaẓah﴾: angels who guard your deeds, and they are the noble scribes (al-kiram al-katibun). It is related from Abu Hatim al-Sijistani that he used to write down from al-Asmaʿi everything he uttered of the benefits of knowledge, until al-Asmaʿi said of him: "You are like the Hafaẓah; you write down every slip of speech." Abu Hatim said: "This too is among the things that are written down."

If you say: God, exalted is He, is self-sufficient in His knowledge and has no need of the angels' recording, so what is the benefit of it? I say: in it there is lutf (divine kindness, grace that draws the servants toward obedience) for the servants. For when they know that God is watching over them, and that the angels, who are the most noble of His creation, are assigned to them, guarding their deeds and recording them in scrolls that will be displayed before the witnesses on the Day of Standing, that is more effective in restraining them from evil and further from wrongdoing.

﴿Tawaffathu rusulunā﴾: meaning, their messengers have fully taken his soul, and they are the Angel of Death and his assistants. It is related from Mujahid: the earth was made for him like a basin (ṭast), so that he takes whomever he takes from it. And there is no household but that he circles around them every day twice.

It has been read as ﴿tawaffāh﴾. It may be both a past and a present verb, in the sense of ﴿tatawaffāh﴾.

﴿Yufarriṭūn﴾ is read with both the doubled and the single letter. Tafrīṭ is slackness and delay beyond the limit, while ifrāṭ is exceeding the limit. That is, they neither diminish from what they were commanded nor add to it.

﴿Thumma ruddū ilā Allāh﴾: that is, to His judgment and His recompense. ﴿Mawlāhum﴾: their master, the one who has authority over their affairs. ﴿Al-ḥaqq﴾: the just, who judges only with truth. ﴿Alā lahu al-ḥukm yawma'idhin﴾: on that Day, no judgment belongs to anyone other than Him. ﴿Wa huwa asraʿu al-ḥāsibīn﴾: He is the swiftest of reckoners, whom no account preoccupies from another account.

It has been read ﴿al-ḥaqqa﴾ in the accusative, as praise, like your saying: "Praise be to God, the True."

Darkness of the land and the sea: a metaphor for their dangers and terrors. It is said of a severe day, "a dark day" and "a day with stars," meaning its darkness has intensified until it becomes like night. It is also permissible that what is meant is: the sinking into the earth on land and drowning at sea, which they fear and dread because of their sins; so when they call upon God and humbly beseech Him, God removes from them the sinking and the drowning, and they are saved from the darkness of both. "If You save us" [is understood with] the implied "saying" (al-qawl) — "from this" (min hadhihi), meaning from this severe darkness. It is also read yunajjikum (with tashdid and takhfif, i.e., doubled and single-consonant forms), and anjana. And khufyatan, with ḍamm and kasr (i.e., with the vowel u and i).

He is the One who has power (al-Qadir): the One you have known to be powerful, the One whose power is complete. Able to send a punishment (ʿadhaban) upon you from above, as He rained stones upon the people of Lut and upon the companions of the Elephant (aṣḥāb al-fīl), and sent the flood upon the people of Nuh; or from beneath your feet, as He drowned Pharaoh and caused Qarun to be swallowed up by the earth. And it has been said: "from above you" means from your great ones and your rulers, and "from beneath your feet" means from your lowly ones and your slaves. And it has been said: it is the withholding of rain and plants. Or to confuse you into factions (shiyaʿan), mixing you into separate groups with divergent desires, each group following a leader. The meaning of "mixing them" is that fighting breaks out among them, so they become confused and entangled in the fierce battles, from the saying of the poet:

"A battalion I have mixed with another battalion, until, when they were entangled, I shook my hand free of them,
So I left them, the spears breaking their backs, among one who is thrown down and another who is propped up.
The lamentation of their women did not benefit me, and I was slain before their men, and ruin is not far off."

He is boasting of being a stirrer of strife who knows its entrances and exits. He says: many a company I have mixed with another, until, when their mixing was complete, I freed myself from them and left them in confusion and bewilderment. But in this there is an affirmation of a trace of baseness. "Shaking the hand" is a metaphor for freeing oneself. Al-waqs means pounding and breaking. Al-mungaʿir is one wounded by an arrow, whose strength is cut off, from al-ʿaqr, which means cutting. It is also narrated as "munʿafir" with a fāʾ, meaning covered with dust. Al-musnad is the passive participle, meaning fallen, some lying prone and some leaning on others. "Wa-la tabʿad" is the speech of the mourning women, a word that women say at a calamity, meaning "may they not perish." His saying "wa-qatalt" is a circumstantial clause: the situation being that I have slain before the men of those women, that is, in front of them, or among them, sufficient for me against them. That is: had I been patient I would have killed them, and the lamentation of their women and their grief over me, together with the safety of their men, did not sway me.

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I asked Allah not to send upon my community a punishment from above them or from beneath their feet, and He gave me that. And I asked Him not to make their violence among themselves, but He refused me, and Jibril informed me that the destruction of my community will be by the sword." [Al-Tha'labi mentioned it like this without a chain. It occurs in several hadiths without the report of Jibril. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Qays from a man, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, 'Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you...' the Prophet (ﷺ) said: he performed ablution, then said: O Allah, do not send upon my community a punishment from above them or from beneath their feet, and do not make them confused in factions. It has corroborating reports: among them in Muslim from Saʿd, traced to the Prophet: "I asked my Lord not to destroy my community by drowning, and He granted it to me. And I asked Him not to make their violence among themselves, and He refused it." In Muslim there is a lengthy hadith from Thawban. In ʿAbd al-Razzaq there is a lengthy hadith from Shaddad ibn Aws as well. In the Muwatta' from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "prayed for his community that no enemy from outside would overcome them, nor would He destroy them by famine, and this was granted; and he prayed that their violence not be among themselves, and this was refused." In Ibn Majah there is a hadith from Muʿadh similar to Saʿd's; al-Nasa'i has one from Anas similar to it; al-Tirmidhi has one from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt similar to it; Ahmad has one from Abu Basra al-Ghifari similar to it; and in al-Tabarani from Ibn ʿAbbas. "There is a fixed time (mustaqarr)," a time of settling and occurrence that cannot be avoided. It has been said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 68–69:

﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse.﴾ They plunge into (yakhuḍūna) into discussion of Our verses, mocking them and disparaging them. The Quraysh used to do this in their assemblies. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, do not sit with them, and rise from them ﴿until they engage in a different discourse﴾. Then there is no harm in sitting with them at that time. ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾, and if he preoccupies you with his whisperings so that you forget the prohibition against sitting with them ﴿then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people﴾, after you have been reminded of the prohibition. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: and if Satan preoccupies you with his whisperings until you forget the prohibition... etc." Ahmad said: This second interpretation aims to apply the rule of good and evil being known by reason, and that reason is sufficient even if no revealed law has come regarding prohibition or other rulings, when they are clear to reason. Such as sitting with mockers, whose ugliness is evident to reason, so reason independently prohibits it. Where revelation has come with this, it discloses its ruling and is based upon it, not originating a ruling in it. You have known the corruption of this principle and its contradiction to the Sunni creed. Moreover, the verse rejects it, for if the forgetting intended here were forgetting the ruling that reason indicates before this prohibition was revealed, it would not have used the future form in "wa-immā yunsiyannaka." Since it came in the future form, there is no basis for taking it as past. And God is the one who grants success.]] It was also read as "yunassinaka" with doubling.

It may also be meant: and if Satan causes you to forget, before the prohibition, the ugliness of sitting with mockers, since reason rejects it, ﴿then do not sit, after the reminder﴾, after We have made you aware of its ugliness and alerted you to it, ﴿with them﴾. ﴿And upon those who are godfearing there is nothing of their reckoning﴾, that is, nothing for which the godfearing who sit with them will be held accountable regarding their sins, ﴿but a reminder﴾, rather it is incumbent upon them to remind them ﴿when they hear them plunging into discourse﴾, by rising from them, showing their displeasure with them, and admonishing them, ﴿so that they may be godfearing﴾, so that they may avoid the plunging into discourse out of shame or out of displeasure at offending them. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to those who are godfearing, meaning they remind them, desiring that they remain steadfast in their piety and increase in it. It is reported that the Muslims said: "If we rise every time they mock the Qur'an, we will not be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque or perform tawaf," so they were granted a concession. If you ask: what is the position (maḥall) of "dhikrā"? I say: it may be in the accusative, as in: "but they remind them a reminder," meaning a reminding. And it may be in the nominative, as in: "but upon them is a reminder."

It is not permissible for it to be a conjunction with the position of "min shay'", as in your saying: "There is no one in the house but Zayd," because His saying "min ḥisābihim" prevents that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿They took their religion as play and amusement﴾: that is, their religion, which they were obligated to adopt, [they took] as play and amusement. This is because the idol-worshippers, and what they practised, such as the prohibition of the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit) and the sa'iba (a free-roaming animal), and other such things, were of the category of play, amusement, following one's whims, and acting on desire, and of the kind of jest rather than earnestness. They took what was play and amusement, namely the worship of idols and other things, as their religion. Or [it means] they took their religion, which was imposed on them and to which they were called, namely the religion of Islam, as play and amusement, since they mocked it and ridiculed it. It was also said: Allah made for every people a festival which they honour, in which they pray and which they fill with the remembrance of Allah. All the people, from among the polytheists and the People of the Book, took their festival as play and amusement, except the Muslims, who took their festival as Allah had prescribed it.

The meaning of ﴿Leave them﴾ is: turn away from them, do not care about their denial and mockery, and do not occupy your heart with them. ﴿And remind [them] thereby﴾: that is, with the Qur'an, ﴿lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, for fear that it be handed over to destruction and punishment, and be held in pledge for what it has earned. The root meaning of ibsal is prevention, because the one who is handed over is held back. [The poet] said:

"My handing over my sons, without any crime,
They were pledged, nor for blood shed."

[This is by Awf ibn al-Ahwas al-Bahili. Ibsal means handing over to the brave one (basil), that is, the courageous one who prevents and frowns. Al-bu'a, with the unpointed 'ayn, means crime. He laments the handing over of his sons to the Bani Qushayr as a pledge for the blood of a man of theirs named Abu al-Sahifa. "Without any crime" means without a sin committed by me and my sons. From this comes the expression: "This is forbidden to you (ʿalayka basl)," that is, unlawful and prohibited. The basil is the brave one, because he refuses to yield to his opponent, or because he is very stern. It is said: the man frowned (basara) when his frown intensified, and when it intensified further they said: basil. The ʿabis is one whose face is contracted.

﴿And though it offer every ransom, it will not be taken from it﴾: that is, though it offer every compensation, it will not be accepted from it. The adl is the ransom. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when his son Abd al-Rahman invited him to worship idols. [Mahmud said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, when his son Abd al-Rahman invited him to worship idols..." Ahmad said: Whoever denies the jinn and their dominion over some people by the power of Allah, so that they suffer seizures, convulsions, and the like, is among those whom the devils have led astray in the wastelands of philosophical misguidance, bewildered, having companions among the monotheists who call him to the lawful guidance, saying "come to us," while he rides in the error of speculative fancies, not turning to them or paying them heed. Sometimes he says that what is reported in the Law about this is imagination, as has already been mentioned in surah al-Baqarah. Sometimes he counts it among the fabrications and embellishments of the Arabs. We have already set out this matter in al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran with a sufficient and eloquent discussion, so renew your commitment to it. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verse 71:

Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured away in the earth, bewildered, [wandering] lost?" ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured away in the earth, bewildered, [wandering] lost?"﴾

[[His saying "al-ardh al-muhmah" (the desert wasteland): that is, the vast desert. Reported from al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari). (ʿ)]] "in the earth, al-muhmah": the vast wilderness; "bewildered": lost, astray from the beaten path, not knowing what to do. "Whom the devils have lured away": that is, the jinn-devils and the ghouls have carried him off. "He has companions": a travelling party who call him to the guidance, that is, to show him the straight road. Or the straight path is called "guidance." They say to him, "Come to us," while he has gone off across the wilderness, following the jinn, and does not answer them or come to them. This is built upon what the Arabs claimed and believed: that the jinn lure a person and the ghouls take possession of him, as in His saying, ﴿those who are driven to madness by the touch of Satan﴾. So the one who strays from the path of Islam, following the steps of Satan, while the Muslims call him to it, and he does not heed them, is likened to this. ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance; and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ That is, Islam is the guidance alone, and whatever lies beyond it is misguidance and error. ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him.﴾ ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of the kaf in His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have lured away﴾? I say: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ﴿nuradd ʿalā aʿqābinā﴾ ("be turned back on our heels"). That is: "Shall we turn back, likened to one whom the devils have lured away?"

If you ask: what is the meaning of istahwathu (has lured away)? I say: it is istifʿāl, from hawā fi al-ardh, when one goes off into the earth. It is as if its meaning were: he sought its desire (hawā) and was eager for it.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of ﴿umirnā﴾ ("we have been commanded")? I say: it is in the accusative, coordinated on the position of the phrase ﴿inna hudā Allāh huwa al-hudā﴾ ("indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance"), on the basis that both are things said. It is as if it were said: "Say this statement, and say, 'We have been commanded [to submit] so that we may submit.'"

If you ask: what is the meaning of the lam in ﴿li-nuslima﴾ ("so that we may submit")? I say: it expresses the reason for the command, meaning: "We were commanded and told: submit, so that we may submit."

If you ask: if this was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, [then how is it that...] — [the commentary continues here in the gloss:] He said: "If you ask: if this was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, how was it said to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿Say, 'Shall we call upon, besides Allah...'﴾ and so on?" Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: This is based on the premise that the command is the will, or that willing the commanded thing is among its necessary implications, and this grammatical analysis is made to fit his (al-Zamakhshari's) belief. As for Ahl al-Sunna (the adherents of the Sunna), as you have learned, the command, in their view, is other than the will and does not necessitate it. Their statement about this lam is like their statement regarding ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they may worship Me﴾, from those who deny that it expresses causation. The way to understand this is that when the clear signs had been made plain to them, and the excuses removed from them, and they were enabled to submit and to worship in compliance with the command, they were treated as those for whom that was willed, as an enablement that urges them to comply and cuts off their excuses when the act willed of them is done for them. What is the case of one who wills something, when he is able to bring it about, except that he removes the obstacles and lifts the impediments? So He dealt thus with the responsible persons, even though obedience was not willed from all of them. As for when the lam is the one that accompanies the verbal noun (maṣdar), as al-Zajjaj says, its estimated form is "the command for submission," and similarly he says regarding the words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾: the will is for the clarification, and it is the lam that accompanies the object when it is fronted, as in your saying, "For Zayd I struck [him]." On this reading it needs no interpretation. It has also been said that it means "an" (that), as if it were said: "and we were commanded that we submit." This is what the speaker of this view said. And the lam of kay (li-kay) is specific to "amarta" (you commanded) and "aradta" (you willed), in the sense of "an" (that), not in its original sense of causation. The purpose of its inclusion is to convey the futurity in a more secure and more emphatic manner, since these two meanings, namely the command and the will, relate only to a future matter. And the three particles, lam, kay and an, have been combined in his saying: "I wanted, so that, that it might fly ..." [the verse of poetry as cited]. This aspect also keeps the meaning free from the flaw that al-Zamakhshari believes, and preserves the creed. We have found the path to this, by the praise of Allah, to be determined. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Then how was it said to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, "Say, 'Shall we call upon...'"? I say: because of the close bond that existed between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers, especially between him and the Companion Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿Qawluhu al-haqq﴾ [His word is the truth] is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). ﴿Yawma yaqulu﴾ [on the day He says] is its predicate (khabar), placed before it. Its accusative case is by way of the sense of temporal specification (istiqra', i.e., the sense of "whenever"), as in your saying: "Friday is the fighting day." The word "al-yawm" here means "the time" (al-hin).

The meaning is: He created the heavens and the earth standing upon the truth and wisdom, and at the time He says to a thing, "Be," and it is, that thing is His word of truth and wisdom. That is, nothing of the heavens and the earth and the rest of created beings comes into being except through wisdom and rightness.

﴿Yawma yunfakhu﴾ [on the day the Trumpet is blown] is an adverbial complement (zarf) of His saying ﴿wa lahu al-mulk﴾ [and His is the dominion], like His saying ﴿li-man al-mulk al-yawm﴾ [To whom belongs the dominion today?].

It is also permissible that ﴿qawluhu al-haqq﴾ be the agent (fa'il, the doer) of ﴿yakun﴾ [it is], in the sense: "and at the time He says to His word, which is true, that is, to His true decree, 'Be,' it is His word of truth."

The accusative of "al-yawm" is governed by an omitted verb, indicated by His saying ﴿bi-l-haqq﴾ [with truth], as if it were said: "and at the time He brings into being and determines, He stands with the truth" ...

﴿'Alim al-ghayb﴾ [Knower of the unseen] is: He is the Knower of the unseen. Its nominative case is by way of praise.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 74–79:

Āzar is the name of Abraham's father, peace be upon him. In the books of history, his name in Syriac is Tārah. The closest view is that the pattern of Āzar is fā'il, like Tārah, ʿĀbir, ʿĀzar, Shālakh, Fālagh, and similar names of theirs. It is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to his father. It was also read as "Āzar" with a ḍamma, as a vocative. It has been said that "Āzar" is the name of an idol, and so he may have been called by it because he was constantly worshipping it, just as Ibn Qays was nicknamed "al-Ruqayyāt" after the women he used to write love poetry about, and so he was called "Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt." In the poetry of one of the later poets:

"I am called by the name 'Asmā' as an insult among her tribes, as if 'Asmā' had become one of my names."

[[He means: they call me by the word "Asmā'" as an insult among her tribes, that is, the tribes of the beloved. In this there is istikhdām (a figure in which one word carries two meanings). "As if Asmā'," that is, this word, has become one of my names. According to Sībawayh, the origin of Asmā' is Wasmā', from wasāma, which means beauty and comeliness. Its initial wāw was changed to a hamza contrary to analogy, as in aḥad. According to al-Mubarrad, it is the plural of ism. Between Asmā' and Asmā'ī there is perfect paronomasia (jinās tāmm, two words identical in form but different in meaning).

On the basis that the ya' is the first person pronoun, it is of the defective type.]]

Or the intended meaning is "the worshipper of Āzar," so the modifier was deleted and the modified term was put in its place. It was also read as "a-Āzaran" (ءأزر), with a fatḥa or kasra on the hamza after the interrogative hamza, a silent zāy, and a fatḥa-ended, tanwīn-marked rā', and it is the name of an idol. Its meaning is: "Do you worship Āzar in denial?" Then he said: "You take idols as gods," as confirmation and affirmation of that. This falls under the ruling of denial, since it serves as its explanation.

Fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-layl ("When the night covered him") is a conjunction on "qāla Ibrāhīm li-abīhi" ("Abraham said to his father").

[[Al-Zamakhshari says: "His saying 'fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-layl' is a conjunction on 'qāla Ibrāhīm li-abīhi'... etc." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: In inserting this sentence there is an indication of what will come concerning Abraham's inference, that it was guidance from God Most High and an alignment with the right path.]]

His saying "wa-kadhālika nurī Ibrāhīm" ("And thus We showed Abraham") is a parenthetical sentence placed between the conjoined and the conjoined-to. The meaning: "In the same way as this instruction and insight, We make Abraham know and see." Malakūt al-samāwāt wa-al-arḍ ("the dominion of the heavens and the earth"): this means lordship and divinity. We enabled him to know it, and guided him by what We opened his breast to and what We made his sight correct, and We showed him the way of inference.

Wa-liyakūna min al-mūqinīn ("and that he might be among those who have certainty"): We did that. "Wa-nurī" is a narration of a past state. His father and his people were worshipping idols, the sun, the moon, and the stars. So he wanted to alert them to the error in their religion, to guide them to the way of reflection and inference, and to make them understand that correct reflection leads to the conclusion that none of these can be God, because there is evidence of their origination (ḥudūth) in them, that behind them is one who originated them, a maker who made them, and a manager who directed their rising, setting, movement, course, and all their conditions.

Hādhā rabbī ("This is my lord"): this is the saying of one who is fair to his opponent while knowing that he is in error. He recounts his words as they are, without partisanship for his own school, because this is more conducive to truth and safer from disputation. Then he turns against it after relating it, refuting it with proof.

Lā uḥibbu al-āfilīn ("I do not love those that set"): I do not love worshipping lords who change from one state to another, who move from place to place, who hide themselves by a veil, for that is a characteristic of heavenly bodies.

Bāzighan ("rising"): beginning to rise.

La-in lam yahdinī rabbī ("Unless my Lord guides me"): an alert to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, and it is similar to the star in setting, is misguided, and that guidance to the truth is by God's grace and kindness.

Hādhā akbar ("This is greater"): this is also from the practice of fairness toward opponents (istiʿmāl al-nuṣfa maʿa al-khuṣūm).

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words continue: "And his saying 'This is greater' is also from the practice of fairness with opponents... etc." Aḥmad says: Al-Zamakhshari is right; indeed that is necessarily the case. The hadith about intercession has come down that people will come to Abraham, peace be upon him, asking him for intercession, and he will say: "My soul, my soul, I ask no one but myself," and he will mention his three lies and say: "I am not fit for it." He means his saying to Sarah, "She is my sister," and by this he meant in religion. And his saying, "I am sick," and by this he meant his concern for his people and their polytheism, and a believer is distressed by that. And his saying, "Rather, it was their chief who did it," and in this there are several indirect allusions. If he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, counted these words against himself while knowing that he will not be held accountable for them, this shows that they were the greatest of what came from him. Thus if the matter were as is claimed, that this speech is related from him as reasoning about himself, it would be more fitting for him to count it greater than what we have mentioned, because then it would be doubt, rather, certainty. Moreover, the correct view is that prophets before prophethood are protected from such things.]]

Innī barīʾ mimmā tushrikūn ("Indeed I am free from what you associate"): from the heavenly bodies that you make partners with their Creator.

Innī wajjahtu wajhiya lilladhī faṭara al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ ("Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth"): that is, to the One to whom these originated things point, and to whom they point as their originator and innovator. It has been said that this was his reflection and inference within himself, which God related.

The first view is more evident, because of His saying, "Unless my Lord guides me," and His saying, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."

If you ask: why did he argue against them with setting rather than rising, when both are a transition from one state to another? I answer: Argument from setting is more evident, because it is a transition with concealment and hiding.

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words continue: "If you ask: why did he argue against them with setting rather than rising, though both are transitions from one state to another?..." Aḥmad says: This is also one of the finest points and excellences.]]

If you ask: what is the reason for the masculine form in His saying "hādhā rabbī," with the pointing to the sun? I answer: the subject is made like the predicate, because both refer to one thing, as in the saying: "mā jāʾat ḥājatuka" (your need did not come) and "man kānat ummuka" (who was your mother). "Lam takun fitnatuhum illā an qālū" ("Their trial was only that they said") — choosing this method was obligatory to protect the Lord from the suspicion of femininity. Do you not see that they said in describing God "ʿAllām" and did not say "ʿAllāmah," although ʿAllāmah is more intensive, to avoid the feminine marker.

It was also read: "tarā Ibrāhīm malakūt al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ," with the tā' and the nominative on malakūt. Its meaning: "You see Abraham the proofs of lordship."

It was also read: "tarā Ibrāhīm malakūt al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ," with the tā' and the nominative on malakūt. Its meaning: "You see Abraham the proofs of lordship."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 6, verses 74–79:

Āzar is the name of Abraham's father, peace be upon him. In the books of history, his name in Syriac is Tārah. The closest view is that the pattern of Āzar is fā'il, like Tārah, ʿĀbir, ʿĀzar, Shālakh, Fālagh, and similar names of theirs. It is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to his father. It was also read as "Āzar" with a ḍamma, as a vocative. It has been said that "Āzar" is the name of an idol, and so he may have been called by it because he was constantly worshipping it, just as Ibn Qays was nicknamed "al-Ruqayyāt" after the women he used to write love poetry about, and so he was called "Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt." In the poetry of one of the later poets:

"I am called by the name 'Asmā' as an insult among her tribes, as if 'Asmā' had become one of my names."

[[He means: they call me by the word "Asmā'" as an insult among her tribes, that is, the tribes of the beloved. In this there is istikhdām (a figure in which one word carries two meanings). "As if Asmā'," that is, this word, has become one of my names. According to Sībawayh, the origin of Asmā' is Wasmā', from wasāma, which means beauty and comeliness. Its initial wāw was changed to a hamza contrary to analogy, as in aḥad. According to al-Mubarrad, it is the plural of ism. Between Asmā' and Asmā'ī there is perfect paronomasia (jinās tāmm, two words identical in form but different in meaning).

On the basis that the ya' is the first person pronoun, it is of the defective type.]]

Or the intended meaning is "the worshipper of Āzar," so the modifier was deleted and the modified term was put in its place. It was also read as "a-Āzaran" (ءأزر), with a fatḥa or kasra on the hamza after the interrogative hamza, a silent zāy, and a fatḥa-ended, tanwīn-marked rā', and it is the name of an idol. Its meaning is: "Do you worship Āzar in denial?" Then he said: "You take idols as gods," as confirmation and affirmation of that. This falls under the ruling of denial, since it serves as its explanation.

Fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-layl ("When the night covered him") is a conjunction on "qāla Ibrāhīm li-abīhi" ("Abraham said to his father").

[[Al-Zamakhshari says: "His saying 'fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-layl' is a conjunction on 'qāla Ibrāhīm li-abīhi'... etc." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: In inserting this sentence there is an indication of what will come concerning Abraham's inference, that it was guidance from God Most High and an alignment with the right path.]]

His saying "wa-kadhālika nurī Ibrāhīm" ("And thus We showed Abraham") is a parenthetical sentence placed between the conjoined and the conjoined-to. The meaning: "In the same way as this instruction and insight, We make Abraham know and see." Malakūt al-samāwāt wa-al-arḍ ("the dominion of the heavens and the earth"): this means lordship and divinity. We enabled him to know it, and guided him by what We opened his breast to and what We made his sight correct, and We showed him the way of inference.

Wa-liyakūna min al-mūqinīn ("and that he might be among those who have certainty"): We did that. "Wa-nurī" is a narration of a past state. His father and his people were worshipping idols, the sun, the moon, and the stars. So he wanted to alert them to the error in their religion, to guide them to the way of reflection and inference, and to make them understand that correct reflection leads to the conclusion that none of these can be God, because there is evidence of their origination (ḥudūth) in them, that behind them is one who originated them, a maker who made them, and a manager who directed their rising, setting, movement, course, and all their conditions.

Hādhā rabbī ("This is my lord"): this is the saying of one who is fair to his opponent while knowing that he is in error. He recounts his words as they are, without partisanship for his own school, because this is more conducive to truth and safer from disputation. Then he turns against it after relating it, refuting it with proof.

Lā uḥibbu al-āfilīn ("I do not love those that set"): I do not love worshipping lords who change from one state to another, who move from place to place, who hide themselves by a veil, for that is a characteristic of heavenly bodies.

Bāzighan ("rising"): beginning to rise.

La-in lam yahdinī rabbī ("Unless my Lord guides me"): an alert to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, and it is similar to the star in setting, is misguided, and that guidance to the truth is by God's grace and kindness.

Hādhā akbar ("This is greater"): this is also from the practice of fairness toward opponents (istiʿmāl al-nuṣfa maʿa al-khuṣūm).

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words continue: "And his saying 'This is greater' is also from the practice of fairness with opponents... etc." Aḥmad says: Al-Zamakhshari is right; indeed that is necessarily the case. The hadith about intercession has come down that people will come to Abraham, peace be upon him, asking him for intercession, and he will say: "My soul, my soul, I ask no one but myself," and he will mention his three lies and say: "I am not fit for it." He means his saying to Sarah, "She is my sister," and by this he meant in religion. And his saying, "I am sick," and by this he meant his concern for his people and their polytheism, and a believer is distressed by that. And his saying, "Rather, it was their chief who did it," and in this there are several indirect allusions. If he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, counted these words against himself while knowing that he will not be held accountable for them, this shows that they were the greatest of what came from him. Thus if the matter were as is claimed, that this speech is related from him as reasoning about himself, it would be more fitting for him to count it greater than what we have mentioned, because then it would be doubt, rather, certainty. Moreover, the correct view is that prophets before prophethood are protected from such things.]]

Innī barīʾ mimmā tushrikūn ("Indeed I am free from what you associate"): from the heavenly bodies that you make partners with their Creator.

Innī wajjahtu wajhiya lilladhī faṭara al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ ("Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth"): that is, to the One to whom these originated things point, and to whom they point as their originator and innovator. It has been said that this was his reflection and inference within himself, which God related.

The first view is more evident, because of His saying, "Unless my Lord guides me," and His saying, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."

If you ask: why did he argue against them with setting rather than rising, when both are a transition from one state to another? I answer: Argument from setting is more evident, because it is a transition with concealment and hiding.

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words continue: "If you ask: why did he argue against them with setting rather than rising, though both are transitions from one state to another?..." Aḥmad says: This is also one of the finest points and excellences.]]

If you ask: what is the reason for the masculine form in His saying "hādhā rabbī," with the pointing to the sun? I answer: the subject is made like the predicate, because both refer to one thing, as in the saying: "mā jāʾat ḥājatuka" (your need did not come) and "man kānat ummuka" (who was your mother).
